overview:
Oghaniryukti (also spelled Ogh‑niryukti, Oghniryukti, Oghaniryūkti) is a classical Jain Prakrit–Sanskrit work belonging to the corpus of niryuktis—early metrical commentaries traditionally attributed to Śrutakevalī Bhadrabāhu Svāmī and later transmitted with bhāṣya and prose vṛtti by subsequent ācāryas such as the Purvācārya and Droṇācārya. It is closely associated with the Avasyakanuyoga (the doctrinal and ritual exposition surrounding the daily obligatory practices, especially sāmāyika) and is counted among the important ancillary texts used to explain and systematize sections of the Śvetāmbara canonical literature.

The text is preserved in multiple recensional forms: a basic niryukti (metre-based Prakrit verses), an attached bhāṣya (explanatory commentary), and an extensive Sanskrit–Prakrit vṛtti (prose and mixed-language exposition) composed by Droṇācārya. Modern printed editions—such as those issued by Agamoday Samiti and later scholarly compilations by Muni Deepratnasāgar—present Oghaniryukti as an integrated work: “mūla (original niryukti) + bhāṣya + Droṇācārya‑vṛtti,” often with editorial introductions that trace its manuscript history and its role in the revival of āgama studies.

Doctrinally, Oghaniryukti belongs to the Avasyakanuyoga and is concerned with the structure, method, and hermeneutics of scriptural study and practice. Early sections discuss the four anuyoga‑dvāras (interpretive gateways)—upakrama (introduction), nikṣepa (categorical placement), anugama (systematic following), and naya (standpoints)—and show how they apply to the study of sāmāyika and other avasyakas. The text distinguishes between niryukti‑anugama (following the metrical commentary) and sūtra‑anugama (following the canonical aphorisms), and elaborates how gateways like uddesa–niddesa (statement and detailed exposition) and various “dvāras” (doors) such as upadhipramāṇa‑dvāra, ālocanā‑dvāra, pratilekhana‑dvāra, anāvartanavarjana‑dvāra, viśodhi‑dvāra, piṇḍa‑dvāra, and pratisevanā‑dvāra organize the practical and textual dimensions of Jain discipline.

Liturgically and pedagogically, Oghaniryukti is used in monastic training and advanced lay study. Some modern introductions note that it is traditionally given or studied in connection with the first day of pravrajyā (initiation into mendicancy), emphasizing its role in framing how a novice understands scriptural authority, confession (ālocanā), textual copying (pratilekhana), and the careful avoidance of repetition and negligence (anāvartanavarjana, viśodhi). The work opens with the standard Jain maṅgala verses, including the Pañcanamaskāra (Namokāra) mantra and a Sanskrit verse saluting Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, and all saṃyatas, thereby situating its discourse within the broader devotional and doctrinal universe of Jainism.

Historically, printed editions of Oghaniryukti have played a significant role in the modern study of Jain āgamas. The 1919 Nirṇaya‑Sāgar Press edition, prepared under the auspices of Agamoday Samiti and based on manuscripts from the Rājanagarīya Vidyāśālā Jñānakośa, helped standardize the text for scholarly and community use. Later compilations, such as “Aagam 41/1 Ogh Niryukti Moolam evam Vrutti” and its inclusion in “Agam Suttani Satikam” alongside Piṇḍaniryukti, further integrated Oghaniryukti into systematic āgama curricula. Contemporary Jain scholars and monks continue to study and teach Oghaniryukti as a key resource for understanding Avasyakanuyoga, scriptural hermeneutics, and the disciplined life of both monks and serious lay practitioners.

Because Oghaniryukti is a layered text—niryukti, bhāṣya, and vṛtti—its interpretation requires attention to the distinction between original metrical formulations, later explanatory expansions, and modern editorial interventions. The niryukti verses often employ dense, technical Prakrit, while the bhāṣya and vṛtti unpack doctrinal terms, ritual procedures, and logical structures. Modern readers are encouraged to consult reliable editions and, where possible, guidance from qualified teachers to navigate variant readings, complex terminology, and the interplay between canonical sūtras and their niryukti‑based exegesis.

primary_sources.title: Śrī Oghaniryukti (mūla, bhāṣya, and Droṇācārya‑vṛtti)
primary_sources.author: Niryukti traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu Svāmī; bhāṣya by Purvācārya; vṛtti by Droṇācārya
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं, णमो आयरियाणं,
णमो उवज्झायाणं, णमो लोए सबसाहूणं,
एसो पंचनमुक्कारो, सङ्घपावप्पणासणो ।
मंगलाणं च सचेसिं, पढमं हवइ मंगलं ॥

दुविहो वक्कमकालो सामायारी अहाउयं चेव ।
सामायारी तिविहा ओहे दसहा पयविभागेण ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arahantāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ, ṇamo ayariyāṇaṃ,
ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, ṇamo loe sabasāhūṇaṃ,
eso paṃcanamukkāro, saṅghapāvappaṇāsaṇo.
maṃgalāṇaṃ ca sacesiṃ, paḍhamaṃ havai maṃgalaṃ.

duviho vakkamakālo sāmāyārī ahāuyaṃ ceva.
sāmāyārī tivihā ohe dasahā payavibhāgeṇa.
primary_sources.translation:
Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas,
homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world.
This fivefold salutation destroys all sins of the saṅgha;
of all auspicious things, it is the foremost auspiciousness.

The time of undertaking (upakrama‑kāla) is twofold: that of sāmāyika and that of confession (ālocanā).
Sāmāyika itself is threefold, distinguished according to the tenfold divisions of its occasions.
primary_sources.notes: These verses occur at the beginning of Oghaniryukti as preserved in printed editions such as the Agamoday Samiti publication (Nirṇaya‑Sāgar Press, 1919) and later compilations. The first passage is the Pañcanamaskāra (Namokāra) mantra, used as a universal Jain maṅgala. The subsequent gāthā introduces the discussion of upakrama‑kāla (the time of initiation) and the classification of sāmāyika within Avasyakanuyoga. The exact wording and segmentation can vary slightly across manuscripts and editions, so readers should treat this as a representative, not critical, text.

primary_sources.title: Oghaniryukti – structural verses on anuyoga‑dvāras
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabāhu Svāmī (traditional attribution) with later vṛtti by Droṇācārya
primary_sources.original_text:
उपक्रमो निक्खेपो अनुगमो नयो इति ।
उद्देसो निइद्देसो य इत्यादि द्वारगाथा ।
primary_sources.transliteration:
upakramo nikkhepo anugamo nayo iti.
uddeso niiddeso ya ityādi dvāragāthā.
primary_sources.translation:
Introduction (upakrama), categorical placement (nikṣepa), systematic following (anugama), and standpoint (naya)—thus (are named).
“Statement and detailed exposition” (uddesa and niddesa), and so on, are the gateway‑verses.
primary_sources.notes: These concise formulations summarize the four anuyoga‑dvāras that structure scriptural study in Avasyakanuyoga. Oghaniryukti uses such gāthās as ‘dvāra‑gāthā’—gateway verses—through which the subsequent bhāṣya and vṛtti elaborate the hermeneutical method. The wording here reflects commonly cited lines in modern editions; minor orthographic differences (e.g., niddesa/niiddesa) occur across recensions.

primary_sources.title: Agam 41/1 Ogh Niryukti Moolam evam Vrutti
primary_sources.author: Compiled by Muni Deepratnasāgar; based on earlier editions and manuscripts
primary_sources.translation:
“I” (the text) am Oghaniryukti—
endowed with the niryukti composed by the venerable Bhadrabāhu Svāmī,
accompanied by the bhāṣya composed by the venerable Purvācārya,
adorned with the vṛtti arranged by the illustrious Droṇācārya,
which refines the Navāṅgī‑vṛtti and is an ornament of the lineage of exegetes.
primary_sources.notes: This self‑descriptive colophon appears on the title or introductory page of modern printed editions, summarizing the layered nature of Oghaniryukti. It is not part of the ancient canonical sūtras but reflects the traditional understanding of authorship and transmission: Bhadrabāhu as niryukti‑kāra, an unnamed Purvācārya as bhāṣya‑kāra, and Droṇācārya as vṛtti‑kāra. The phrase ‘navāṅgī‑vṛtti‑śodhaka’ indicates the role of Droṇācārya’s work in clarifying and refining earlier commentarial traditions on the nine aṅgas.

misconceptions.myth: Oghaniryukti is itself a primary canonical sūtra on the same level as the main aṅgas and upāṅgas.
misconceptions.reality: Oghaniryukti is a niryukti—an early metrical commentary—linked to Avasyakanuyoga and transmitted with bhāṣya and vṛtti. While highly respected and traditionally attributed to the Śrutakevalī Bhadrabāhu, it functions as an exegetical and pedagogical text rather than as one of the core canonical aṅga or upāṅga sūtras. Its authority is therefore interpretive and traditional, not identical to that of the principal āgama sūtras.

misconceptions.myth: Oghaniryukti is only a ritual manual for monks and has no relevance for lay practitioners.
misconceptions.reality: Although Oghaniryukti is deeply embedded in monastic training—especially in the context of pravrajyā and Avasyakanuyoga—it also addresses general structures of scriptural study, confession, textual care, and sāmāyika that are meaningful for serious lay practitioners. Modern teachers often draw on its classifications of dvāras and anuyoga‑methods to explain how both monks and laypeople can approach Jain texts and practices systematically.

misconceptions.myth: There is a single, universally fixed text of Oghaniryukti without any variation or editorial layering.
misconceptions.reality: Surviving manuscripts and printed editions show that Oghaniryukti exists in layered and sometimes variant forms: niryukti verses, attached bhāṣya, Droṇācārya’s vṛtti, and later editorial introductions. Different publishers and compilers (e.g., Agamoday Samiti, Jain āgama projects, and individual monks) have produced slightly different recensions. Responsible study therefore pays attention to edition history, variant readings, and the distinction between ancient metrical material and later explanatory or editorial additions.
